summaryEn: One of the world's three largest silicon-wafer makers — the raw material every chip is built on, sitting upstream of TSMC. A capital-intensive oligopoly cyclical now two-thirds below its 2023 earnings peak, with its dividend cut from NT$25 to NT$7.7, while building a strategically vital US footprint backed by CHIPS Act money and a Micron supply deal.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + TPEx/press; silicon-wafer framing — global top-3 position, US CHIPS-backed expansion, Micron anchor deal and recovering quarterly trend credited, but the ~66% earnings collapse from peak, dividend cut NT$25 → 7.7, thin trough margins, the failed Siltronic bid, heavy capex and a ~65x multiple on depressed profits stated plainly; net-above-operating margin flagged as non-operating income with the cause hedged; market corrected TWSE → TPEx)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
GlobalWafers (環球晶圓, TPEx: 6488) makes the thing every other semiconductor company in this collection depends on: **the silicon wafer itself**. It sits **upstream of TSMC, UMC and Nanya** — the supplier of the polished discs on which all chips are fabricated — and is **one of the world's three largest wafer makers**, with a portfolio spanning **300mm silicon** and **8-inch silicon-carbide (SiC) substrates**. It was **spun out of Sino-American Silicon's semiconductor division in October 2011** and **listed in September 2015**.

Its recent record is a **deep cyclical downturn from a spectacular peak**. Annual EPS ran **NT$35.30 (FY2022) → NT$45.41 (FY2023, the peak) → NT$21.17 (FY2024) → NT$15.30 (FY2025)** — a fall of roughly **two-thirds**. The dividend has been cut just as hard: from **NT$25.0 (2018–2019)** to **NT$19.0 (2023), NT$11.0 (2024) and NT$7.7 (2025)**. Gross margin compressed from **30.1% to 20.8%** and operating margin from **21.9% to 10.6%**, with revenue still marginally negative year-on-year. The **quarterly trend, however, has been recovering**: EPS went **NT$0.87 (2024Q4) → 3.05 → 3.52 → 4.12 → 4.61 → 3.97 (2026Q1)**.

Two strategic threads define the company. The first is a **failure**: in November 2020 it bid nearly **NT$130bn for Germany's Siltronic** — the **largest acquisition ever attempted by a Taiwanese technology company** — and the deal **collapsed when German government approval did not arrive**. The second is a **success in progress**: its **US expansion**, where plants in **Sherman, Texas and St. Peters, Missouri** secured a **US CHIPS Act direct subsidy of up to US$406m** plus advanced-manufacturing tax credits, **Micron invested US$500m and signed a 10-year supply agreement**, and a further **US$4bn investment** has been announced. The honest read: **a genuinely top-three global supplier of an indispensable material, in the trough of a capital-intensive commodity cycle, building strategically vital Western capacity with government support — but trading at ~65× depressed earnings with an 8.3% return on equity.**

GlobalWafers exists because of a deliberate corporate separation. Its parent, **Sino-American Silicon (中美矽晶)**, had built both a solar-wafer business and a semiconductor-wafer business; in **October 2011** the semiconductor division was **spun out as a standalone company**, GlobalWafers, so that it could pursue its own strategy and capital. It **listed in September 2015**.

What followed was one of the most aggressive consolidation campaigns in Taiwanese industry. Silicon wafers are an **oligopoly** — a handful of suppliers worldwide serve every chipmaker — and scale is decisive because the business is enormously **capital-intensive** and technically demanding, particularly at **300mm** and at the leading edge of flatness, purity and defect control. GlobalWafers grew by **buying its way up the league table**, acquiring wafer businesses internationally until it stood **among the global top three**, and extended into **8-inch silicon-carbide substrates** for power electronics and electric vehicles.

The campaign's climax was also its defeat. In **November 2020** GlobalWafers launched a **near-NT$130bn bid for Germany's Siltronic** — the **largest M&A ever attempted by a Taiwanese tech company** — which would have created a clear global number two. The deal **failed for want of German government approval**, a reminder that in an era of semiconductor nationalism, wafer capacity is treated as strategic infrastructure rather than a tradeable asset.

Denied consolidation, the company pivoted to **building rather than buying — in the West**. Its **Texas and Missouri** plants, supported by **US CHIPS Act funding** and anchored by **Micron's US$500m investment and 10-year supply agreement**, are an attempt to become the domestic wafer supplier for America's semiconductor rebuild — the same strategic logic that blocked Siltronic, now working in its favour.

- **2011 (18 Oct)** — Incorporated as a **spin-off of Sino-American Silicon's semiconductor wafer division**.
- **2015 (25 Sep)** — **Lists on the TPEx (over-the-counter) market (6488)**.
- **2010s** — Grows by international acquisition into the **global top three** silicon-wafer suppliers; adds **8-inch SiC substrates**.
- **2020 (Nov)** — Bids nearly **NT$130bn for Germany's Siltronic** — the **largest attempted M&A by a Taiwanese tech company**.
- **2022** — The Siltronic deal **fails** for want of German government approval; FY2022 EPS **NT$35.30**.
- **2023** — **Peak earnings: EPS NT$45.41**; dividend NT$19.0.
- **2024** — Downturn begins: EPS falls to **NT$21.17**; dividend cut to **NT$11.0**. **US Commerce Department awards up to US$406m** in CHIPS Act direct subsidy for the **Sherman (Texas)** and **St. Peters (Missouri)** plants.
- **2025** — EPS **NT$15.30** (≈one-third of the peak); dividend cut again to **NT$7.7**. **Micron invests US$500m** in the Texas plant with a **10-year supply agreement**; the Texas plant opens and a further **US$4bn** investment is announced.
- **2026Q1** — Gross margin 20.8%, EPS **NT$3.97**; quarterly earnings recovering off the 2024Q4 low of NT$0.87.

GlobalWafers' accounts are those of a **capital-intensive oligopolist in a cyclical trough**, with one detail worth flagging.

- **A collapse from an exceptional peak.** Annual EPS **NT$35.30 (FY2022) → 45.41 (FY2023) → 21.17 (FY2024) → 15.30 (FY2025)**. Gross margin fell from **30.1% (2024Q4) to 20.8% (2026Q1)** and operating margin from **21.9% to 10.6%** as utilisation and pricing weakened. **ROE is now only ~8.3%**.
- **A dividend cut to match.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$25.0 (2018 and 2019) → 18.0 → 16.0 (2021–2022) → 19.0 (2023) → 11.0 (2024) → 7.7 (2025)**. At NT$959 the yield is just **~0.72%** — this is not an income stock in its current phase.
- **A heavily invested balance sheet.** A **~55.8% debt ratio** on **NT$211bn of assets**, against **NT$93.4bn of equity** and **NT$24.1bn of cash**. Wafer plants cost billions and take years; the US expansion adds further multi-year capital commitments (a further **US$4bn** announced), partly offset by **CHIPS Act subsidies of up to US$406m** and advanced-manufacturing tax credits.
- **An earnings-quality note.** **Net margin (13.56%) exceeds operating margin (10.55%)** in 2026Q1, and did so by a wide gap in 2025Q3 (13.6% versus 8.5%) — meaning **significant non-operating income**. Government incentives associated with the US expansion are a plausible contributor, but the specific composition is not something the headline data settles; the practical implication is that **operating margin, not net margin, is the cleaner measure of the core business** right now.
- **A valuation that prices recovery.** **P/E ~65.7×** on trough earnings and **P/B ~5.45×** — expensive on today's profits, and dependent on the cycle turning.

The financing reality: **a soundly financed, strategically important manufacturer spending heavily through a downturn** — the balance sheet can carry it, but the earnings and dividend show how brutal the wafer cycle is.

**Stance: a global top-three supplier of an indispensable material, in a cyclical trough, building strategically favoured Western capacity — priced at ~65× depressed earnings on the expectation the cycle turns. Quality position, demanding entry price.**

The bull case:

1. **An oligopoly position in a material nobody can do without.** Silicon wafers are the substrate of every chip; only a handful of firms can supply them at leading-edge quality. GlobalWafers is **top three globally**, with **300mm silicon and 8-inch SiC** for power and EV applications.
2. **A strategically privileged Western footprint.** **Texas and Missouri** plants backed by **up to US$406m of CHIPS Act direct subsidy** and tax credits, **anchored by Micron's US$500m investment and a 10-year supply agreement**. In a world where wafer capacity is treated as strategic infrastructure — the very reason its Siltronic bid was blocked — being the **US-based wafer supplier** is a durable advantage.
3. **A recovering trend.** Quarterly EPS has climbed from **NT$0.87 (2024Q4) to NT$3.97 (2026Q1)**, suggesting the worst of the destocking is past.

The counter-arguments are substantial:

- **The scale of the fall.** EPS is **roughly two-thirds below the FY2023 peak**, and the **dividend has been cut from NT$25 to NT$7.7** — this cycle has been severe, and revenue is still marginally negative year-on-year.
- **Thin trough economics.** Operating margin of **~10.6%** and **ROE of ~8.3%** on a capital-intensive asset base is a poor return; the business only looks good at mid-cycle or better.
- **Heavy, committed capital expenditure.** A further **US$4bn** of US investment must be funded and earned back, whatever the cycle does.
- **A ~65× multiple on trough earnings** with a **0.72% yield** offers no support if recovery is delayed.

A **cyclical-recovery** thesis: an excellent structural position bought at a price that already assumes normalisation.

GlobalWafers makes money by **growing, slicing, polishing and selling silicon** — a business that is simple to describe and extremely hard to do:

- **Silicon wafers (the core).** It grows single-crystal silicon ingots, slices them into wafers, and polishes them to extraordinary tolerances of flatness, purity and defect density. **300mm wafers** for advanced logic and memory are the highest-value product; smaller diameters serve mature nodes, analog, power and sensors. Customers are **every foundry, IDM and memory maker** — the wafer is the first input in the entire chain.
- **SiC substrates (the growth option).** **8-inch silicon-carbide** substrates for power electronics, electric vehicles and industrial applications — a materially different, faster-growing market where the technical barrier is higher and the supplier set smaller.
- **Long-term agreements.** Because wafer capacity takes years to build and chipmakers cannot risk shortages, supply is often contracted years ahead — **Micron's 10-year agreement** for Texas output is the clearest example. This dampens, but does not eliminate, cyclicality.

The economics are those of a **capital-intensive oligopoly**. Plants cost billions, run best at full utilisation, and carry heavy depreciation — so **margins swing violently with utilisation and pricing**. In an upturn, incremental volume drops almost entirely to the bottom line (FY2023's NT$45.41 EPS); in a downturn, fixed costs crush margins (FY2025's NT$15.30, with operating margin at ~10.6%). The levers are **utilisation, wafer pricing, product mix (300mm and SiC versus mature diameters), and capital-expenditure discipline**. The strategic overlay is **geography**: with governments now subsidising domestic wafer capacity, **where you build matters as much as how well you build** — which is why the US expansion, and the government money attached to it, is central to the investment case.

Silicon wafers are the **most concentrated layer of the semiconductor supply chain** — and increasingly a matter of national policy.

- **A tight global oligopoly.** A handful of suppliers — Japan's **Shin-Etsu** and **SUMCO**, Germany's **Siltronic**, Korea's **SK Siltron**, and **GlobalWafers** — provide essentially all the world's semiconductor-grade silicon. Barriers are extreme: crystal-growth know-how, decades of process refinement, customer qualification measured in years, and billions in capital per plant. New entrants effectively do not appear.
- **Brutally cyclical.** Because capacity is added in large, slow increments while chip demand swings quickly, wafer prices and utilisation **overshoot in both directions**. The 2022–2023 boom and the 2024–2025 collapse in GlobalWafers' earnings are the same phenomenon that has recurred for decades.
- **Now strategic infrastructure.** The failure of the **Siltronic acquisition** — blocked for want of German approval — showed that governments no longer treat wafer capacity as an ordinary asset. The corollary is the **US CHIPS Act**, which is paying GlobalWafers up to **US$406m** to build in **Texas and Missouri**, with **Micron** underwriting demand for a decade. Wafer suppliers are being courted by the same politics that constrained them.
- **SiC is a different race.** Silicon-carbide substrates for EVs and power electronics are growing faster, with a distinct competitive set (Wolfspeed, Coherent, Chinese entrants) and their own pricing pressure.

GlobalWafers' position is **structurally strong but cyclically exposed**: it is one of very few companies that can supply what the industry cannot function without, and one of the few positioned to do so **inside the United States** — yet it earns an **8.3% ROE** at the bottom of the cycle. The industry truth is that **wafer making is a wonderful oligopoly and a terrible commodity at the same time**, and which one you experience depends entirely on where you stand in the cycle.

**Strengths**
- **Global top-three** silicon-wafer supplier — an oligopoly with near-insurmountable entry barriers.
- **Strategically favoured US footprint**: Texas and Missouri plants with **up to US$406m of CHIPS Act subsidy**, tax credits, and **Micron's US$500m investment plus a 10-year supply agreement**.
- **Broad portfolio**: 300mm silicon for advanced nodes plus **8-inch SiC** for power/EV; solid balance sheet (NT$93.4bn equity, NT$24.1bn cash).

**Weaknesses**
- **Severe cyclical downturn**: EPS **NT$45.41 → 15.30 (−66%)**; dividend **NT$25 → 7.7**; **ROE only ~8.3%**.
- **Thin trough margins** (operating ~10.6%) on a very capital-heavy asset base.
- **Expensive valuation** (~65.7× trough earnings, ~0.72% yield); net-above-operating margin means reported profit leans on non-operating items.

**Opportunities**
- **Cycle recovery** — quarterly EPS already up from NT$0.87 to NT$3.97; AI and advanced-node demand for 300mm.
- **US onshoring** making it the domestic wafer supplier of choice; further government support.
- **SiC growth** in EVs and power electronics.

**Threats**
- Prolonged wafer oversupply or price competition, including from **Chinese entrants**.
- **US$4bn of committed capex** to fund through an uncertain cycle.
- Geopolitical constraints (as the **blocked Siltronic deal** demonstrated) and customer concentration in long-term contracts.

- **Cyclicality (the defining risk).** Wafer earnings swing violently: EPS fell from **NT$45.41 to NT$15.30** in two years while operating margin halved to ~10.6%. A slower recovery would leave a ~65× multiple stranded on depressed profits.
- **Capital-expenditure commitment.** A further **US$4bn** of US investment must be spent and recovered regardless of the cycle; wafer plants take years to build and ramp, so capital is committed long before revenue appears.
- **Valuation and yield.** At **~65.7× earnings, ~5.45× book and a 0.72% yield**, the stock offers little downside protection while earnings are depressed.
- **Earnings quality.** **Net margin exceeds operating margin**, so reported profit currently benefits from **non-operating items**; the operating line is the more conservative measure of the core business.
- **Geopolitical dependence, in both directions.** Government policy blocked the **Siltronic acquisition** and is now funding the **US plants** — a reminder that strategic politics can help or hinder, and that subsidy programmes carry conditions and timing risk.
- **Competition and technology.** Established Japanese and Korean rivals, plus subsidised Chinese entrants in mature diameters and SiC, pressure pricing; SiC in particular is seeing rapid capacity additions.

GlobalWafers' outlook rests on two clocks running at different speeds: **the wafer cycle, which is short and violent, and the onshoring build-out, which is long and strategic.** The axes to watch:

- **Cycle recovery in utilisation and pricing.** The near-term driver — whether the quarterly improvement (EPS **NT$0.87 → 3.97**) continues into rising **gross margin** (now 20.8%, versus 30.1% at the 2024 peak quarter) and a return to revenue growth. Margin, not headline revenue, is the honest gauge.
- **The US ramp.** Whether **Sherman, Texas** and **St. Peters, Missouri** ramp on schedule and profitably, with **CHIPS subsidies (up to US$406m)** and the **Micron 10-year agreement** underwriting the risk. Success would make GlobalWafers structurally more valuable than its cycle position suggests.
- **SiC.** Whether **8-inch silicon-carbide** substrates scale into a meaningful second business as EV and power-electronics demand matures — and whether pricing holds against rapid capacity additions.
- **Capital discipline and the dividend.** Funding **US$4bn** of expansion while earnings are depressed; whether the dividend, cut from **NT$25 to NT$7.7**, stabilises as cash flow recovers.

Bottom line: GlobalWafers supplies **the material on which the entire semiconductor industry is built**, from a **global top-three position** that new entrants cannot realistically challenge, and is becoming **America's domestic wafer supplier** with government money and a **10-year Micron contract** behind it. But it is also a **capital-intensive commodity cyclical** currently **two-thirds below its earnings peak**, with a **dividend cut by 70%**, **~10.6% operating margins**, an **8.3% ROE**, and a **~65× multiple on trough profits**. Judge it on **utilisation and gross margin, the US ramp, and SiC** — an outstanding structural asset whose share price already assumes the cycle behaves.
